questions.stem: An article explains that a local park was renovated to include a new playground and a community garden. The main purpose is to create a safe space for children and families. Which of the following details from the article should be included in a summary?
questions.successCriteria: Identifies the core supporting detail vs. irrelevant detail.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can distinguish between core supporting details and trivial details in a summary.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks every specific descriptive detail is important.

options.label: A
options.text: The playground has a blue slide and a red climbing frame.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a specific trivial detail that does not support the main idea. Summaries should focus on core functional details.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: Cost is not the core idea here; the main purpose is safety and recreation. Include only explicitly stated core details.

options.label: C
options.text: The new playground and community garden provide safe recreational areas for children and families.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This captures the core purpose of the renovation.

options.label: D
options.text: The park is located near the downtown area.
options.feedbackWrong: Location is not the core idea; the article's focus is on the renovation's purpose.

questions.stem: When writing a summary of a news article, which of the following sentences would be acceptable?
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can avoid personal opinion in summaries.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks including personal opinion is acceptable in summaries.

options.label: A
options.text: The government's decision to fund the project is a great move.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a personal opinion. Summaries should only present facts from the source, not judgments.

options.label: B
options.text: The article states that the government decided to fund the project.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is an objective reporting of what the article says.

options.label: C
options.text: I think the project will benefit the community.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a personal opinion. Avoid first-person expressions.

options.label: D
options.text: The government should have funded a different project.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a personal opinion. Summaries should not include recommendations.

questions.stem: You are summarizing a magazine story about the benefits of urban green spaces. Which of the following would be appropriate to include in the summary?
questions.successCriteria: Identifies content solely from the source vs. external knowledge.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student avoids including external connections or background knowledge not in the source.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks it is okay to bring in outside facts or personal associations.

options.label: A
options.text: The author mentions that green spaces improve air quality, which is supported by my science class.
options.feedbackWrong: This connects to external knowledge (science class). Summaries must only contain information from the source text.

options.label: B
options.text: Green spaces are also popular in other countries like Japan.
options.feedbackWrong: This is an external connection not mentioned in the article. Do not add facts from outside.

options.label: C
options.text: The article's main idea is that urban green spaces provide health and environmental benefits.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is directly from the article's content.

options.label: D
options.text: This reminds me of the park near my house.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a personal connection. Summaries should be objective and not include personal references.

questions.stem: A source sentence: 'The study concluded that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.' Which of the following would be an acceptable paraphrase for a summary?
questions.successCriteria: Selects a proper paraphrase that restates the idea in new words without changing meaning.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can paraphrase rather than copy verbatim.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks copying a few words or changing one word is acceptable paraphrasing.

options.label: A
options.text: The study concluded that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
options.feedbackWrong: This is copied verbatim from the source. You must paraphrase in your own words.

options.label: B
options.text: Regular exercise, according to the study, lowers the chance of heart disease.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This rephrases the idea using different wording while preserving the meaning.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: This is too vague and loses the specific claim from the study. A paraphrase must keep the key information.

options.label: D
options.text: The study's conclusion: regular exercise reduces heart disease risk.
options.feedbackWrong: This is still too close to the original wording; 'reduces heart disease risk' is not sufficiently paraphrased.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picked wrong option on Q1
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that every specific descriptive detail from the text is important to include in a summary, even if it is trivial or unrelated to the main idea.

miniLesson.explain: A summary must include only the explicit core main idea and the supporting details that directly validate it. Trivial details—like a creation year or color of equipment—do not belong because they do not help the reader understand the text's central point. Ask yourself: 'Does this detail help explain the main idea? If I remove it, does the main idea still make sense?' If yes, it may be important; if no, leave it out.
miniLesson.example: Consider an article about a sculpture that helps preserve sand dunes against rising seas. A correct summary would state the sculpture's core function (preserving dunes). An incorrect summary would mention the year it was created—that detail is interesting but irrelevant to the main idea.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Core function, not flashy fact: focus on the 'why' not the 'what color'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this sentence: 'The park renovation included a new playground with a blue slide and a red climbing frame, and a community garden to provide safe recreational areas for children and families.' Which detail is essential to include in a summary?
guidedPractice.answer: The correct answer is: 'new playground and community garden provide safe recreational areas for children and families.' The colors of the slide and frame are trivial details.

guidedPractice.prompt: Choose the better summary for an article whose main idea is that a local library expanded to offer free adult literacy programs. Option A: 'The library added a new wing with modern furniture, opened in 2022, and now offers free adult literacy programs to help residents improve reading skills.' Option B: 'The library expansion includes free adult literacy programs to help residents improve reading skills.'
guidedPractice.answer: Option B is better because it focuses on the core function (adult literacy programs) and omits the trivial detail of the year opened and furniture type.

guidedPractice.prompt: Imagine you are summarizing a news article about a new community center. The article says: 'The center, built with $5 million in donations, features a basketball court, a computer lab, and a weekly job fair that has already helped 30 people find work. The building's exterior is made of red brick.' Write a one-sentence summary that includes only the core supporting details.
guidedPractice.answer: The new community center, funded by $5 million in donations, includes a basketball court, computer lab, and a weekly job fair that has helped 30 people find work.

reteachModules.trigger: Student includes personal opinions or unstated inferences in a summary.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think it is acceptable to add their own judgments, feelings, or inferred ideas beyond what the source explicitly states.

miniLesson.explain: Summaries must be objective and only include information explicitly stated in the source text. Personal opinions (e.g., 'The author makes a great point') and unstated inferences (e.g., assuming the creator is an environmentalist) are prohibited. Use a formal, neutral tone without first-person pronouns.
miniLesson.example: In class, the correct summary stated 'the sculpture's core function is preserving dunes against rising seas.' The incorrect version said 'the creator must be an environmentalist,' which is an unstated inference.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: No I, no We, no Feel—just explicit Facts.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following sentences is objective and could be in a summary? A) 'The article's main idea is that renewable energy reduces emissions.' B) 'I believe renewable energy is the best solution.'
guidedPractice.answer: A

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this opinionated sentence as an objective fact suitable for a summary: 'The new policy is a wonderful step forward for the environment.'
guidedPractice.answer: The article states that the new policy is intended to benefit the environment.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify and correct the subjective or inferential content in this summary excerpt: 'The author presents data on rising temperatures. Unfortunately, they ignore the economic impact. This shows they are biased.'
guidedPractice.answer: Remove 'Unfortunately, they ignore the economic impact' (opinion) and 'This shows they are biased' (inference). Correct version: 'The author presents data on rising temperatures but does not discuss the economic impact, according to the source.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q3
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student mistakenly includes connections to other texts or personal background knowledge that are not present in the source text, violating the rule that summaries must only contain information explicitly stated in the original.

miniLesson.explain: In non-fiction summaries, you must include only information that is directly stated in the source text. Do not add connections to other texts, personal experiences, or outside knowledge. For example, if an article discusses the benefits of urban green spaces, you cannot mention that 'similar parks exist in Japan' unless that fact is in the article. Summaries should be self-contained and objective.
miniLesson.example: Original text: 'Urban green spaces improve air quality and provide recreational areas.' Incorrect summary addition: 'This is similar to the park near my house.' Correct summary: 'The article states that urban green spaces improve air quality and offer recreation.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of the summary as a closed box: only what comes from the source goes inside. No outside items allowed.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following would be acceptable to include in a summary? (A) The author mentions that green spaces improve air quality. (B) Green spaces are also common in Japan, which I learned in geography. (C) This reminds me of a documentary I saw. (D) I think green spaces are great.
guidedPractice.answer: A (only A comes from the source text).

guidedPractice.prompt: You are summarizing an article about the benefits of meditation. The article says: 'Meditation reduces stress and improves focus.' Which of the following is appropriate to include in the summary? (A) Meditation is also used in schools. (B) The article explains that meditation reduces stress and improves focus. (C) Many celebrities meditate. (D) I find meditation relaxing.
guidedPractice.answer: B (only B restates the source content without external connections).

guidedPractice.prompt: A student writes a summary of a news report about a new recycling program. The summary includes: 'The program aims to reduce waste, similar to the program in my hometown.' What rule does this violate? Explain why it is incorrect and rewrite the sentence correctly using only information from the report.
guidedPractice.answer: This violates the rule against external connections. The student added personal background knowledge not in the source. Corrected version: 'The program aims to reduce waste.' (or similar direct restatement).

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects a verbatim copy or near-copy of the source text as an acceptable summary sentence.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students believe that copying the original wording is acceptable, as long as it is accurate. They do not understand that a summary must restate ideas in their own words to demonstrate understanding and avoid plagiarism.

miniLesson.explain: A summary must be entirely in your own words. Paraphrasing means rephrasing the original idea using different vocabulary and sentence structure while keeping the same meaning. Simply changing a few words or swapping synonyms is not enough; you must restructure the sentence and use your own language.
miniLesson.example:
Source: 'The study concluded that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.'
Poor paraphrase (too close): 'The study concluded that regular exercise reduces heart disease risk.'
Good paraphrase: 'According to the research, engaging in physical activity on a regular basis lowers the likelihood of developing heart conditions.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of 'Paraphrase = Paint a new picture with the same story.' You keep the meaning but change the words completely.

guidedPractice.prompt: Source sentence: 'The new policy requires all students to wear uniforms.' Rewrite this sentence in your own words without copying more than two consecutive words from the original.
guidedPractice.answer: The updated rule makes it mandatory for every student to dress in uniforms.

guidedPractice.prompt: Source: 'Because of the heavy rainfall, the outdoor event was postponed until next week.' Paraphrase this for a summary, using completely different wording and structure.
guidedPractice.answer: A significant amount of rain caused the postponement of the outdoor activity, which is now rescheduled for the following week.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this short paragraph: 'Scientists have discovered a new species of frog in the Amazon rainforest. The frog is bright blue and has a unique call. Researchers believe its bright color warns predators of its toxicity.' Write a one-sentence paraphrase that captures the main idea without copying any phrase verbatim.
guidedPractice.answer: Researchers found a new blue-hued Amazonian frog that uses its vivid color and distinctive call as an alert to potential threats about its poisonous nature.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q5
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student uses first-person or second-person pronouns (e.g., I, you, we) in summaries instead of a formal, objective tone.

miniLesson.explain: Summaries must be written in a formal, objective tone. This means you must avoid using first-person pronouns (I, me, my, we, our) and second-person pronouns (you, your). The focus should be on the source text's information, not your perspective or the reader's. Including 'I think' or 'you can see' makes the summary subjective and informal, which is not allowed. Only use third-person (he, she, it, they) or refer to the source itself.
miniLesson.example:
Incorrect: 'I believe the article shows that the sculpture is important.'
Correct: 'The article argues that the sculpture serves a key function.'
Incorrect: 'You can see that the park has many benefits.'
Correct: 'The park provides several benefits, according to the source.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: No I, You, or We in summaries. Keep it third-person and objective.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following sentences uses the correct formal tone for a summary? A) 'I think the author’s main point is clear.' B) 'The author’s main point is that exercise improves health.'
guidedPractice.answer: B

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this sentence to remove the first-person pronoun: 'In my opinion, the study shows that reading helps vocabulary.'
guidedPractice.answer: The study shows that reading helps vocabulary.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a one-sentence summary of this statement using a formal, objective tone: 'Our team worked hard, and I think you will agree that our results are impressive.' (From a company blog)
guidedPractice.answer: The company blog states that the team's hard work led to impressive results.

reteachModules.trigger: Student uses an AI translation tool or AI-generated content instead of conducting the interview in English.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think that using AI or translation tools saves time and still produces original work, not realizing the assignment requires a genuine English conversation and that any AI assistance violates academic integrity.

miniLesson.explain: Unit 2 Assignment 1 requires you to conduct an original interview in English with an English-speaking school community member. The interview must be recorded, and you must ask at least three unplanned follow-up questions based on the W5H framework. Using AI translation tools or AI-generated content goes against the assignment's purpose of developing authentic English communication and writing skills. It is considered academic dishonesty and can result in a score of zero. The interview must be spontaneous and in English, not pre-translated or AI-assisted.
miniLesson.example: Incorrect: Writing interview questions in Chinese, translating them with Google Translate, and then reading them to the interviewee. Correct: Preparing English questions, conducting the interview in English, and asking unplanned follow-up questions naturally during the conversation.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: English-only, no AI, no translation. Think of it as a live conversation where you must think on your feet.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sara is preparing for her interview. She writes her questions in Chinese and uses an AI tool to translate them into English. She plans to read the translated questions. Is this acceptable? Why or why not?
guidedPractice.answer: No, because using translation tools violates the assignment rule that all work must be based on actual interviews conducted in English. The interview must be spontaneous and original.

guidedPractice.prompt: During the interview, your partner (interviewee) speaks entirely in English. You feel nervous and think of using a translation app to understand their answer. What should you do? Explain two reasons why using the app would be wrong.
guidedPractice.answer: You should not use the app. First, the interview must be conducted entirely in English, and using a translation tool means you are not interacting in English naturally. Second, the assignment prohibits AI-assisted content; it undermines the purpose of practicing English communication.

guidedPractice.prompt: Imagine you are giving feedback to a peer who used AI to polish their interview narrative before submission. Write three sentences explaining why this is problematic and what they should do instead.
guidedPractice.answer: Using AI to polish your narrative is not allowed because the assignment requires all work to be your own based on the actual interview. It risks academic penalties. Instead, you should revise your own writing using the writing process: draft, self-edit, and get feedback from a teacher or peer.

reteachModules.trigger: You did not record your interview. Without a recording, your assignment receives a score of zero.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think they can rely on memory or notes, or that the recording is optional, but the assignment explicitly requires audio/video recording as proof of an authentic interview. Without it, the assignment cannot be evaluated and receives a zero.

miniLesson.explain: Recording is mandatory because it provides evidence that the interview was conducted in English with a real person, that you asked follow-up questions, and that no AI or translation was used. A missing recording results in an automatic score of zero, as per the assignment rubric.
miniLesson.example: A student named Maya completed her interview and wrote a great narrative, but forgot to record. She submitted her work, but the teacher could not verify that the interview happened or that it was in English. Maya received a zero for the assignment.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: RECORD = RESULT. If you don't press record, you get a zero.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: If you have good notes from the interview, you don't need to record it.
guidedPractice.answer: False. The assignment requires an audio/video recording. Notes are not sufficient.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your classmate says they forgot to record but promises it was a great interview. What should you tell them?
guidedPractice.answer: You should remind them that the assignment requires a recording; without it, they will get a zero. They need to redo the interview with recording.

guidedPractice.prompt: Imagine you are about to start your interview. List the three key things you must do to ensure you don't lose points due to recording issues.
guidedPractice.answer: 1. Check that your recording device (phone/laptop) has enough battery and storage. 2. Clearly ask the interviewee for permission to record. 3. Press record before starting the interview and verify it is recording.

reteachModules.trigger: You conducted part of the interview in Chinese.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: I thought it was okay to switch to Chinese when the interviewee struggled, as long as most of the interview was in English.

miniLesson.explain: The assignment requires the entire interview to be conducted in English. Using any other language, even partially, violates the assignment rules and results in a score of zero. This is because the task assesses your ability to communicate in English and produce an original narrative based on an English-only interaction.
miniLesson.example: A student interviewed a school librarian. The first two questions were in English, but when the librarian paused, the student asked the next question in Chinese. The recording showed this language switch, and the student received zero credit for the assignment.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: All English, all the time — zero tolerance for non-English.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: It is acceptable to ask a few questions in a language other than English during the interview, as long as the main language is English.
guidedPractice.answer: False

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this transcript excerpt: Student: 'Can you tell me about your favorite book?' Interviewee: 'Sure, I love mysteries.' Student: '为什么你喜歡神秘故事?' Which part of the interview violates the English-only rule?
guidedPractice.answer: The student's third line ('为什么你喜歡神秘故事?') is in Chinese and violates the rule.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following mixed-language interview segment entirely in English, keeping the same meaning: Student: 'What inspired you to become a teacher?' Interviewee: 'My high school English teacher.' Student: '那太棒了! Can you tell me more about her?'
guidedPractice.answer: Student: 'What inspired you to become a teacher?' Interviewee: 'My high school English teacher.' Student: 'That's wonderful! Can you tell me more about her?'

reteachModules.trigger: You did not include at least 3 unplanned follow-up questions in your interview.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think that simply following a script or only asking pre-planned questions is sufficient, or they do not know how to generate follow-up questions that deepen the interview.

miniLesson.explain: Follow-up questions are spontaneous questions you ask based on what the interviewee just said. They show active listening and help uncover deeper stories. The W5H framework (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How) is a useful tool for generating them. For example, if the interviewee says 'I moved to Canada in 2015,' you could ask 'Why did you decide to move?' or 'How did you feel about the move?' The assignment requires at least 3 unplanned follow-up questions using W5H.
miniLesson.example: Interviewee: 'I started volunteering at the animal shelter because I love dogs.' Follow-up: 'What kind of dogs do you work with?' or 'How has volunteering changed your perspective?'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: W5H are your tools for digging deeper.

guidedPractice.prompt: Interviewee says: 'I enjoy reading science fiction novels.' Write one follow-up question using W5H.
guidedPractice.answer: What do you like most about science fiction?

guidedPractice.prompt: Interviewee says: 'I moved to Toronto for university. The city was overwhelming at first.' Write two follow-up questions using W5H.
guidedPractice.answer: Why was it overwhelming? How did you adjust to the city?

guidedPractice.prompt: Interviewee says: 'I started my own business last year. It was tough because I had no prior experience, but I learned a lot about marketing and customer service.' Write three unplanned follow-up questions using W5H.
guidedPractice.answer: What inspired you to start the business? What was the biggest challenge you faced? How did you learn about marketing?

questions.stem: Read the following text: 'The new community garden, opened in 2023, features rows of vegetables and a small greenhouse to provide fresh produce for local families.' Which detail should be excluded from a summary?
options: The garden opened in 2023.
The garden provides fresh produce for local families.
The garden has vegetable rows and a greenhouse.

questions.stem: Write a one-sentence summary of the text below that includes only the core main idea and essential supporting details, excluding trivial or irrelevant details. Text: 'A local artist painted a mural on Main Street in 2024. The mural depicts colorful birds and flowers, and aims to bring attention to the need for urban green spaces. The artist used acrylic paint and worked for two months.'
questions.rubric: Summary must: (1) state the mural's purpose to bring attention to urban green spaces, (2) mention the depiction of birds and flowers as supporting detail, (3) exclude the year (2024), paint type (acrylic), and duration (two months). Acceptable example: 'A local artist painted a mural of birds and flowers to bring attention to the need for urban green spaces.'

retestCards.passRule: Both questions answered correctly; Q2 must meet rubric criteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences would be acceptable in a summary because it is objective and factual?
options: The author argues that urban parks improve mental health, citing survey results.
I think urban parks are a wonderful idea for city residents.
The author makes a compelling case for urban parks, which is obviously true.
Urban parks are clearly the best solution for city stress.

questions.stem:
Rewrite the following sentence to make it objective and suitable for a summary, removing any personal opinion or inference:

'The government's new education plan is a fantastic initiative that will finally fix our schools.'
questions.rubric: The rewritten sentence must state only what the source explicitly says, without value judgments or assumptions. Acceptable: 'According to the article, the government's new education plan aims to improve schools.' or similar. Must avoid words like 'fantastic', 'finally', 'fix' as subjective or inferential. Full credit for an objective paraphrase of the source's claim.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct objective sentence (q1) and produce a rewritten sentence free of personal opinion and unstated inference (q2). Partial credit allowed on q2 if minor issues remain, but overall must demonstrate clear understanding of the rule.

questions.stem: When summarizing a text, which of the following is acceptable to include?
options: Information directly stated in the source
Connections to other texts you have read
Personal experiences related to the topic
Your opinion about the topic

questions.stem: You are summarizing an article about the health benefits of walking. The article states: 'Walking for 30 minutes daily reduces the risk of heart disease and improves mental health.' A student's summary includes: 'Walking is good for you, just like the jogging program I started last year.' Identify the error and write a corrected sentence that only uses information from the article.
questions.rubric: The student must point out that the summary includes an external connection (the jogging program) not in the article. The corrected sentence should be something like: 'The article states that walking 30 minutes daily reduces heart disease risk and improves mental health.'

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer Q1 correctly and Q2 must correctly identify the error and provide a corrected sentence that only uses source information.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best paraphrase of the sentence: 'The OUTLINE method is a 7-step process for writing summaries.'
options: The OUTLINE method is a 7-step process for writing summaries.
To write summaries, the OUTLINE method involves seven steps.
The OUTLINE method, which is a process for writing summaries, has 7 steps.
A summary can be written using the 7-step OUTLINE method.

questions.stem: Paraphrase the following sentence in your own words: 'Summaries must avoid personal opinions and unstated inferences.'
questions.rubric: The response must: (1) convey the same meaning (2) use different words and sentence structure (3) not copy more than two consecutive words from the original. Acceptable example: 'When writing a summary, one should not include their own opinions or ideas that are not directly stated in the source text.'

retestCards.passRule: Answer the multiple-choice correctly AND write an open-ended paraphrase that meets the rubric criteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is written in the correct formal tone for a summary?
options: I believe the experiment proves that the new drug is effective.
The experiment proves that the new drug is effective, according to the study.
You can see from the data that the new drug works well.
We think the experiment shows the drug's effectiveness.

questions.stem:
Rewrite the following sentence so that it uses a formal, objective tone suitable for a summary. Remove all first-person and second-person pronouns.

"In my opinion, you can clearly see from the article that the city's new policy will reduce traffic."
questions.rubric: The response must be a single sentence that restates the original idea using third-person references only (e.g., 'the article', 'the city's policy'). It must avoid words like 'I', 'me', 'my', 'we', 'our', 'you', 'your'. The meaning should be preserved: that the article indicates the policy will reduce traffic. Example: 'The article states that the city's new policy will reduce traffic.'

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an acceptable way to prepare for the English interview?
options: Write your questions in English and practice them aloud.
Write your questions in Chinese and use Google Translate to convert them.
Use ChatGPT to generate a list of interview questions.
Ask a friend who speaks Chinese to translate your questions.

questions.stem: Explain why using an AI translation tool during the interview violates the assignment requirements. Provide two reasons.
questions.rubric: Student must mention: (1) The interview must be conducted entirely in English; translation means you are not interacting in English naturally. (2) The assignment prohibits AI-assisted content; it is considered academic dishonesty and may result in a score of zero.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: A student completed an interview and has detailed notes, but forgot to record. They ask you what to do. Which advice is correct?
options: Submit the notes as proof instead of a recording.
Explain that without a recording, the assignment will receive a zero and they need to redo the interview with a recording.
Ask the interviewee to write a letter confirming the interview happened.
Write a note to the teacher explaining the mistake.

questions.stem: You are about to start your interview. Describe three specific steps you must take to ensure your interview is properly recorded and avoids a zero score.
questions.rubric: Must include at least two of the following key steps: 1) Check device battery and storage; 2) Ask permission to record; 3) Press record before starting and verify it is recording.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: What is the rule about language use in the interview assignment?
options: The interview must be conducted entirely in English; any use of another language results in a score of zero.
It is acceptable to use another language for a few questions as long as most of the interview is in English.
The interview can be conducted in any language, but the final narrative must be written in English.
Using a translation app to convert questions to English is allowed.

questions.stem:
Read this excerpt from a student interview. The student used some Chinese. Rewrite the entire excerpt so that it follows the English-only rule and keeps the same meaning.

Student: 'What is your favorite memory from high school?'
Interviewee: 'Graduation day, when I received my diploma.'
Student: '那一定很激动。Can you describe that moment?'
Interviewee: 'Yes, it was very emotional.'
questions.rubric: The response must be entirely in English, with the Chinese phrase replaced by an equivalent English expression (e.g., 'That must have been exciting' or 'That must have been emotional'), and the meaning must be preserved. The entire conversation must use only English.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly: the single-choice must select the correct option (index 0), and the open-ended response must be entirely in English and preserve the original meaning.

questions.stem: During an interview, the interviewee says: 'I started a community garden because I wanted to bring neighbors together.' Which of the following is an example of an effective unplanned follow-up question using the W5H framework?
options: What year did you start the garden?
How do you think the garden has changed relationships in the neighborhood?
Do you like gardening?
Have you always lived in this neighborhood?

questions.stem: Imagine you are interviewing a classmate who just said: 'I joined the school's debate club last semester. It was challenging at first because I had to speak in front of many people, but now I feel more confident.' Write at least three unplanned follow-up questions using the W5H framework (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How).
questions.rubric: The response must include at least 3 questions that are clearly follow-ups to the given statement and use the W5H framework. Each question should be distinct and relevant.

retestCards.passRule: Student must correctly answer the multiple-choice question (option 1 is correct) AND generate at least 3 appropriate follow-up questions using W5H in the open-ended response.

teacherEscalation.condition: student fails the same retest twice or scores in the lowest tier on two consecutive lesson diagnostics
teacherEscalation.message: 该学生需要人工短辅导；问题不是单题错误，而是核心概念系统没有建立。

dashboardFormat.objective: Summaries must include only the explicit core main idea and supporting details that directly validate it, paraphrased in the writer's own words.；Summaries must use formal, objective tone, avoiding first/second person pronouns.；Prohibited content in summaries: personal opinions, unstated inferences, external text connections, personal background knowledge, and trivial details unrelated to the main idea.

learningGoals.statement: Understand and apply the rules for writing non-fiction summaries, including content selection, paraphrasing, and formal tone.
Understand and apply the 7-step OUTLINE method to summarize informational texts.

Understand and apply the key requirements of Unit 2 Assignment 1: conducting an English-only interview with recording, asking at least 3 unplanned follow-up questions, and writing a 400+ word narrative without AI assistance.

cards.question: An article explains that a local park was renovated to include a new playground and a community garden. The main purpose is to create a safe space for children and families. Which of the following details from the article should be included in a summary?
options: The playground has a blue slide and a red climbing frame.
The park renovation cost $2 million.
The new playground and community garden provide safe recreational areas for children and families.
The park is located near the downtown area.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can distinguish between core supporting details and trivial details in a summary.
misconceptions: This is a specific trivial detail that does not support the main idea. Summaries should focus on core functional details.
Cost is not the core idea here; the main purpose is safety and recreation. Include only explicitly stated core details.
✓ Correct. This captures the core purpose of the renovation.
Location is not the core idea; the article's focus is on the renovation's purpose.
cards.successCriteria: Identifies the core supporting detail vs. irrelevant detail.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks every specific descriptive detail is important.

cards.question: When writing a summary of a news article, which of the following sentences would be acceptable?
options: The government's decision to fund the project is a great move.
The article states that the government decided to fund the project.
I think the project will benefit the community.
The government should have funded a different project.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can avoid personal opinion in summaries.
misconceptions: This is a personal opinion. Summaries should only present facts from the source, not judgments.
✓ Correct. This is an objective reporting of what the article says.
This is a personal opinion. Avoid first-person expressions.
This is a personal opinion. Summaries should not include recommendations.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks including personal opinion is acceptable in summaries.

cards.question: You are summarizing a magazine story about the benefits of urban green spaces. Which of the following would be appropriate to include in the summary?
options: The author mentions that green spaces improve air quality, which is supported by my science class.
Green spaces are also popular in other countries like Japan.
The article's main idea is that urban green spaces provide health and environmental benefits.
This reminds me of the park near my house.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student avoids including external connections or background knowledge not in the source.
misconceptions: This connects to external knowledge (science class). Summaries must only contain information from the source text.
This is an external connection not mentioned in the article. Do not add facts from outside.
✓ Correct. This is directly from the article's content.
This is a personal connection. Summaries should be objective and not include personal references.
cards.successCriteria: Identifies content solely from the source vs. external knowledge.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks it is okay to bring in outside facts or personal associations.

cards.question: A source sentence: 'The study concluded that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.' Which of the following would be an acceptable paraphrase for a summary?
options: The study concluded that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
Regular exercise, according to the study, lowers the chance of heart disease.
It is important to exercise.
The study's conclusion: regular exercise reduces heart disease risk.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can paraphrase rather than copy verbatim.
misconceptions: This is copied verbatim from the source. You must paraphrase in your own words.
✓ Correct. This rephrases the idea using different wording while preserving the meaning.
This is too vague and loses the specific claim from the study. A paraphrase must keep the key information.
This is still too close to the original wording; 'reduces heart disease risk' is not sufficiently paraphrased.
cards.successCriteria: Selects a proper paraphrase that restates the idea in new words without changing meaning.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Direct match to summary writing expectation B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks copying a few words or changing one word is acceptable paraphrasing.
